claims.text: NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 has a critical temperature–strain-rate combination within 673–873 K and 0.0005–0.001 s^-1.
Crossing the critical combination causes a microstructural transition involving increased dislocation density and dynamic clustering or short-range order.
The proposed microstructural transition produces a pronounced change in yield strength.
The proposed microstructural transition produces a pronounced change in thermoelastic modulus.
The specimens will initially be uniform, as-cast and homogenized, with an equiaxed grain structure and minimal pre-existing dislocation density.
The relevant structural evolution is a transition from homogeneous dislocation motion to behavior dominated by increased dislocation density and clustering or local atomic ordering.
High temperature enhances atomic mobility in this alloy under the proposed test conditions.
Enhanced atomic mobility drives a transition in dislocation behavior in which dislocation cores interact more strongly.
Stronger interactions between dislocation cores lead to cluster formation.
The resulting clusters lower the energy barrier for slip.
Lowering the slip barrier reduces yield strength above the critical condition.
The same microstructural reorganization alters the thermoelastic modulus measured by nanoindentation.
Below the critical threshold, the alloy exhibits a uniform yield strength and elastic response.
Above the critical threshold, yield strength decreases significantly and thermoelastic modulus shifts measurably.
Uniform mechanical behavior and no observable dislocation clustering across the tested conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to an inert atmosphere, temperatures of 673–873 K, and strain rates of 0.0005–0.001 s^-1.
The precise onset of clustering may vary because of specimen heterogeneity.
Correlating nanoscale in-situ observations with bulk mechanical responses introduces uncertainty.
